introduction: Today Lent begins. Through the prophet Joel, God calls his people: "turn to me with all your heart." Paul pleads with us to "be reconciled to God," for "now is the day of salvation." In the Gospel, Jesus speaks of the three practices of Lent (almsgiving, prayer, and fasting) and asks us to do them for our Father who sees in secret. The ashes we receive are a sign that we are mortal and need God's mercy. Let us begin these forty days with honest and humble hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. Let us turn to him in prayer.
intentions: For the Church: that this Lent may be a time of true conversion for all her members, beginning with our own hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens preparing for Baptism at Easter: that the Holy Spirit may guide them in these final weeks of preparation. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the poor and the hungry: that our fasting and almsgiving may become real help for those in need. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who carry the weight of sin or shame: that they may hear the call to come back to God, and find his mercy in the sacrament of Reconciliation. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may pray, fast, and give in secret, seeking only to please our Father. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful Father, you call us back to you with all our hearts. Create in us a clean heart, and lead us through these forty days to the joy of Easter. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Tear your heart
reflection.body:
Joel speaks to a people in crisis, and God's word through him is direct: "Yet even now," says the LORD, "turn to me with all your heart." The words "even now" matter. It is never too late. And the turning must be real: "Tear your heart and not your garments." Outward signs mean little unless the heart changes.

Why should we turn back? Joel answers by describing God himself: "he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness." Lent is not about earning God's love. It is about coming home to a love that has been waiting for us.

Paul writes as if he cannot wait: "we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God." And again: "Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation." Not next year, not when life is less busy. Now.

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks about the three practices of Lent: giving alms, praying, and fasting. He does not ask whether we will do them, but how. The danger is doing them to be seen. Three times he says that those who seek praise "have received their reward." Instead he says, "your Father who sees in secret will reward you." Lent is lived mostly in hidden places: in a room with the door shut, in a quiet gift, in a meal given up without fuss.

The ashes on your forehead are the one public sign of this day. Let them remind you that life is short and that God's mercy is great. Choose one way to pray, one way to fast, and one way to give, and pray the psalm each day: "Create in me a clean heart, O God."
